source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Morgan_2012_KetamineUseReview.pdf, pp. 27–38 (all 12 pages, including the reference list). Text layer extracted with pdftotext -layout (born-digital); pp. 27–33 rendered at 150 dpi and pp. 27, 32 and 33 checked on the page images.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. The review itself overstates: it describes the ex-ketamine group as abstinent for at least a year, and describes the 1-year cohort's findings in causal terms (p. 32); the claim rightly does not adopt either.
claims.note: The review is the same team's narrative summary and is cited here only as qualifying context. Its hedged reading of the comparison with people who had stopped (memory impairments may be reversible) fits the claim's 'insufficient ... contested'. Two cautions for the editor: (1) the abstinence of at least a year it states (p. 32, no reference given for that sentence) conflicts with the primary-study figures in the claim (mean 344 days, range 120 to 2980), so the review should not be used for abstinence duration; (2) the causal sentence about the 1-year study cites [30], which the reference list (p. 35) gives as Stewart (2001), 'Ketamine as a street drug', not the longitudinal study [31] (Morgan et al., 2010); it reports the correlations with change in use but not the improvement over the year that the claim describes. Editors' calculation in the claim, '18 of the 57 ketamine participants of two earlier field studies': 20 (Curran & Morgan, 2000) + 18 + 19 (Curran & Monaghan, 2001) = 57 completers reproduces; Curran & Morgan (2000) also tested 7 more people once and dropped 2 (pp. 577–578), so 57 holds only if the follow-up drew on completers.

anchors.locator: Physical and psychological harms › Chronic physical and psychological effects › Cognitive impairment, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Memory impairments are said to be possibly reversible after stopping, because they were not found in a group of 30 people who had stopped using ketamine, described as abstinent for at least a year (no reference for this sentence). In the same paragraph a longitudinal study is said to show that frequent use caused impairments in visual recognition and spatial working memory that correlated with changes in use over 12 months, cited as [30] (Stewart 2001 in the list on p. 35, not the 1-year study, [31]); planning and frontal impairments are said to be unrelated so far to measures of use [11].

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. The review is stronger than its sources in places: 'profound impairments' in short- and long-term memory, and causal wording for the observational 1-year study (p. 32); the claim keeps to association and to some tests, not others.
claims.note: Same team's narrative review, qualifying context only, no numbers taken. It agrees with the claim that infrequent or recreational use does not appear to be associated with long-term cognitive impairment (citing [56], Narendran et al. 2005) and that cross-sectional studies cannot address causation, and says planning and frontal impairments appear unrelated to measures of use [11]. Its abstract (p. 27) says frequent, daily use is associated with neurocognitive impairment, most robustly working and episodic memory. It does not discuss the education, premorbid-ability or family-history differences, or testing within days of last use, that the claim raises; and its causal sentence cites the wrong reference number ([30] instead of [31]).

anchors.locator: Physical and psychological harms › Chronic physical and psychological effects › Cognitive impairment, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Several studies of people using ketamine infrequently and frequently cited ([11,55,56,59–61]); infrequent or recreational use not apparently associated with long-term cognitive impairment [56]; most robust finding called profound short- and long-term memory impairment in people using frequently (for review [57]); many studies cross-sectional and unable to address causation; longitudinal study described in causal terms [30]; planning and frontal impairments observed but so far unrelated to measures of ketamine use [11].
Frequent, daily use said to be associated with neurocognitive impairment, most robustly deficits in working and episodic memory.

claims.overstatement: None. 'Releases dopamine' fairly paraphrases the review's 'induces activation of dopamine release'. Calling the review narrative is fair: it says it searched systematically with a pre-defined evidence hierarchy (p. 27), but gives no selection results and no appraisal of studies.
claims.note: The four extra actions are on p. 27: muscarinic block and possible GABA potentiation without any citation, dopamine release citing [1] and weak mu-opioid agonism citing [2], so 'gives no study for several of these statements' is right. Further support for the claim's caution, from the review itself: [1] is, by its printed title, a commentary asking whether striatal dopamine release after NMDA antagonists can be seen at all (p. 35); of [67–69], cited on p. 33 for human PET evidence of striatal dopamine release, the titles of [67] (prefrontal activation) and [69] (FDG metabolic hyperfrontality) are not dopamine-release studies, only [68] (raclopride) is; p. 33 says ketamine's affinity for mu-opioid and sigma sites is relatively low, and that R-ketamine has a greater opioid action without a citation (the preceding sentence cites [33], a 1978 book). Written on behalf of the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs (p. 27 byline), which fits 'written for a UK scientific committee'.

anchors.extracted: Main action: non-competitive antagonism at the NMDA receptor. Less prominent actions: blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and may potentiate GABA synaptic inhibition (no citations); induces activation of dopamine release [1]; weak agonist at mu-opioid receptors [2]; two optical isomers with differing NMDA affinities.

anchors.locator: Dependence-related harms › Acute pleasure associated with taking the drug › Neurochemical actions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Dopamine rise in rat striatum and prefrontal cortex [66]; some human PET studies said to show striatal dopamine release [67–69] (titles on pp. 36–37: [67] prefrontal activation, [68] raclopride, [69] FDG metabolism). Ketamine interacts with mu-opioid and sigma sites with relatively low affinity; S-ketamine has much greater NMDA affinity and R-ketamine a greater opioid action (no citation for the last statement).

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. The review goes further than the claim: it states that people using infrequently scored higher than polydrug controls on delusions, dissociation and schizotypy [31,55] and that people using daily showed a pattern of 'basic symptoms' like people prodromal for schizophrenia (p. 32), without qualification.
claims.note: Same team's narrative review; qualifying context. It agrees with the claim that the depression rise over a year (Beck Depression Inventory) was in the daily-use and ex-use groups, not in the infrequent-use group, and was not at clinical levels; it adds that the increase was not correlated with changes in ketamine use (pp. 31–32), a point the claim could add because it weakens a causal reading. It also says there is little evidence linking chronic heavy use to a diagnosed psychotic disorder (p. 32), consistent with the claim. Two points for the editor: (1) the review twice defines the infrequent group as more than once a month but under 3 times a week (pp. 31, 32), whereas the claim says 'less than four times a week'; check against Morgan et al. (2009); (2) its support for people using infrequently scoring above controls cites [55], Curran & Morgan (2000), whose measures were state ratings taken 3 days after a night of use.

anchors.locator: Physical and psychological harms › Chronic physical and psychological effects › Depression, 1st paragraph (continues on p. 32)
anchors.extracted: In the team's 1-year study [31], Beck Depression Inventory scores rose in the daily-use and ex-use groups but not in people currently using infrequently (defined as more than once a month, under 3 times a week); the raised scores were not at clinical levels and the increase did not correlate with changes in ketamine use.

anchors.locator: Physical and psychological harms › Chronic physical and psychological effects › Psychosis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Delusions, dissociation and schizotypy scores said to be higher with daily than with infrequent use and with infrequent use than in polydrug controls [31,55]; people using daily showed a basic-symptoms pattern similar to people prodromal for schizophrenia [31]; no evidence of clinical psychotic symptoms with infrequent use [56]; despite anecdotes, little evidence linking chronic heavy use to diagnosis of a psychotic disorder.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. All eight listed gaps check against the pages.

missed: The review describes the 30 people who had stopped using ketamine as abstinent for at least a year (p. 32, no reference), which conflicts with the primary-study figures that cl_ket_cognition_after_stopping gives for Morgan et al. (2009): a mean of 344 days, range 120 to 2980 (to be confirmed on the morgan_2009 card). Key finding 18 and the interpretation gap repeat the year without flagging the conflict.

The review's definition of infrequent use (more than once a month, under 3 times a week; pp. 31, 32; key finding 1) differs from the claims' description of the Morgan et al. (2009) infrequent group (at least monthly, less than four times a week); one of the two is wrong; check against morgan_2009.

Ref. 55 (Curran & Morgan, 2000), cited for people using infrequently scoring above polydrug controls on delusions, dissociation and schizotypy (p. 32), measured state ratings 3 days after a night of use in a group using twice a week to monthly (sc_curran_2000), so the review's statement mixes residual state effects with everyday levels; key finding 16 notes only that intoxication at testing is not stated.
